## Why this paper

. . .

A tension that keeps growing when psychology studies social phenomena: the **i-frame** and the **s-frame** [@chaterIframeSframeHow2023]

. . .

Poverty illustrates it unusually well: a huge, stable, structural problem with a large behavioural-science literature on the individuals in it

. . .

A concrete case for thinking the tension through, rather than in the abstract

::: {.notes}
- Chater and Loewenstein (2023, Behavioral and Brain Sciences): behavioural public policy has framed problems at the level of the individual (i-frame), which has led it astray from the system-level causes and solutions (s-frame). The same tension shows up in climate communication, misinformation, trust in science.
- Brady is a sociologist who makes the s-frame case for poverty without using the term. Sheehy-Skeffington and colleagues (section 4) are psychologists who take the i-frame versus s-frame framing explicitly and try to answer it for poverty.
- Why poverty is a good case: the evidence on both sides is unusually mature. Four decades of cross-national data on the poverty rate, and fifteen years of experiments on decision-making under scarcity.
:::

---

## {.big-center}

::: {.statement}
The field asks why **the poor** are poor.
:::

. . .

::: {.statement}
Brady asks why the United States has so much **poverty**. [@bradyPovertyNotPoor2023]
:::

::: {.notes}
- Review article by David Brady (UC Riverside, WZB Berlin), Science Advances 2023.
- Opens with Katz: "The idea that poverty is a problem of persons ... has dominated discussions of poverty for well over two hundred years and given us the enduring idea of the undeserving poor."
- The field routinely asks why the poor fail to get married, do not complete their education, do not work.
- Brady: this focus "has been incapable of providing an accurate understanding of that systemically high poverty." Needs a paradigm shift: poverty, not the poor.
:::

---

# 1. Systemically high poverty

## How poverty is measured here

. . .

- Relative measure: poor if household income is below 50% of the median

. . .

- Income after taxes, tax credits and transfers ("post-fisc"), equivalised by household size

. . .

- Data: Luxembourg Income Study (LIS), rich democracies, 1980 to 2020

::: {.notes}
- The official US poverty measure (OPM) is explicitly avoided: thresholds too low, based on a 1950s rule of thumb that food is a third of expenses, ignores taxes and tax credits, counts some transfers but not SNAP, housing subsidies, EITC, CTC. Two National Academy panels (1995, 2019) critiqued it.
- Relative measures "better predict well-being, health, and life chances" and are more reliable over time and across places.
- Equivalised: income divided by the square root of household members.
:::

---

## Five patterns

::: {.incremental}
- a huge share of the population
- a perennial outlier among rich democracies
- staggeringly high for certain groups
- unexpectedly high for those who "play by the rules"
- pervasive across groups and places
:::

::: {.notes}
- These five patterns are Brady's definition of "systemically high". One figure for each.
:::

---

## A huge share of the population

![Millions of people in the United States experiencing major social problems (2019 or 2020). Far more people are in poverty than experience more visible problems. Brady (2023), Fig. 1.](figures/fig1.jpeg){.card fig-align="center" width="80%"}

::: {.notes}
- 2019: 17.5% of the US population, about 57.4 million people, were poor.
- Almost 64 times as many people in poverty as evicted. More than 32 times as many as incarcerated. 17 times the victims of violent crime. Almost 10 times the unemployed.
- Pew has never listed poverty among the biggest problems facing the nation.
- Poverty is also an event: about 45 to 46% of people in poverty are in their first year of being poor. About 61% of Americans experience at least one year of poverty in their lives.
:::

---

## A perennial outlier

![Poverty rate in the United States (solid line) and the median of 19 other rich democracies (dashed line, with ± one cross-national SD), 1980–2020. Brady (2023), Fig. 2.](figures/fig2.jpeg){.card fig-align="center" width="85%"}

::: {.notes}
- Solid line: US, every year near its average of 17%. Dashed: median of 18 other rich democracies, average 8.8% over the period.
- "By far, the clearest 'trend' in American poverty is stability at a high level."
- Stability is not an artefact of the relative measure: Israel, Luxembourg, Sweden, UK show substantial change.
- Israel has had higher poverty than the US since 2005. Otherwise the typical rich democracy stays far below.
:::

---

## Staggeringly high for some groups

![Child poverty rates for U.S. ethno-racial groups (2016–2020) and for 30 rich democracies, with 95% CIs. Dashed line: median child poverty rate across the 30 rich democracies. Brady (2023), Fig. 3.](figures/fig3.jpeg){.card fig-align="center" height="490"}

::: {.notes}
- Child poverty. Black children 33.5%, Latino children 29.8%, Native American children 29.4%.
- No rich democracy comes close: the next highest are Israel and Spain at about 22%, and none exceeded 26.1% in four decades of LIS data.
- White and Asian American children are close to the cross-national median of 10.8%. White child poverty is lower than in Canada and France.
- So the US overall rate is partly "simply due to staggeringly high poverty for ethno-racial minorities".
- Backup: Fig. 4, Black and Latino child poverty near 50% in the 1980s.
:::

---

## Unexpectedly high for those who "play by the rules"

![Poverty rates for the overall population and for non-risk groups among working-aged households (HHs), United States (2016–2020) versus the cross-national (CN) median of 31 rich democracies. Dotted line: CN median for the overall population. Brady (2023), Fig. 5.](figures/fig5.jpeg){.card fig-align="center" height="490"}

::: {.notes}
- Non-risk groups among working-aged households, US versus the cross-national (CN) median of 31 rich democracies.
- Employed households: 12.1% in the US, above the CN median for the overall population (10%).
- Households led by a high school graduate: 12.8%. Non-young households (head 25+): 14.4%.
- Even people with zero risks: 7.4% are in poverty.
- And most Americans are not in the risk groups: 94.8% of working-aged households are employed, 91.2% led by someone with at least high school.
- More than three times as many people in working-poor households (9.7% of the population) as in jobless poor households (3.2%).
:::

---

## Pervasive across groups and places

![Poverty rates for age groups, adult women and men, regions and places in the United States (2016–2020). Dotted line: cross-national median poverty rate for the overall population. Brady (2023), Fig. 6.](figures/fig6.jpeg){.card fig-align="center" height="490"}

::: {.notes}
- Highest among under 18s and over 64s, in the South, central cities and rural areas.
- But above the cross-national median among working-aged adults, among both women and men, in all four regions, in large cities, moderate cities and suburbs.
:::

# 2. Three prevailing approaches

## {.big-center}

::: {.statement}
(i) fixing the poor
:::

. . .

::: {.statement}
(ii) dramatizing the poor
:::

. . .

::: {.statement}
(iii) cultural explanations
:::

::: {.notes}
- Brady's own labels. All three focus on the individual poor rather than on why poverty is systemically high. He links this to America's uniquely strong individualistic ideology.
:::

## (i) Fixing the poor

Behavioural explanations: the poor are poor because they more often carry one of four risks

::: {.incremental}
- joblessness
- low education
- young headship
- single motherhood
:::

. . .

Anti-poverty strategy: reduce the share of the population with these risks

::: {.notes}
- Behaviour is the mechanism, driven by choices and incentives, culture, traits. Hence the focus on welfare disincentives, on getting people to marry, finish school, work.
- Example named in the paper: Shah, Mullainathan and Shafir (2012, Science) simulate scarcity in lab games (Wheel of Fortune, Family Feud, Angry Birds) and conclude "the poor often behave in ways that reinforce poverty."
- Public version: Sawhill's "success sequence". AEI-Brookings consensus plans of 2015 and 2022: first recommendation is a new cultural norm around marriage.
:::

---

## (i) Fixing the poor: prevalences and penalties

. . .

**Prevalence**: the share of the population with a risk

**Penalty**: how much more likely a risk makes you to be poor

. . .

The US does not stand out on prevalences. It has the highest penalties of any rich democracy.

::: {.notes}
- Framework from Brady, Finnigan and Hübgen (2017). Three critiques of behavioural explanations:
- (1) Prevalences cannot explain macro variation. Across 29 rich democracies the US ranks 20th on the prevalence of at least one risk, below average on joblessness and low education. If the US had median prevalences, poverty would go up, not down. Risks have declined markedly since the 1970s while poverty stayed flat.
- (2) Causality is questionable. Risk coefficients are not causally identified, risks are endogenous to poverty. Penalties vary over time and across countries: in 16 of 29 rich democracies single motherhood does not even significantly predict working-aged poverty.
- (3) Behaviouralists study prevalences and neglect penalties, yet there is far more variation in penalties, and reducing penalties would reduce poverty more.
- "Who is poor" does not explain "why there is poverty".
- Studying only the US, an outlier on both poverty and penalties, biases impressions about how much risks matter. Smeeding: the US literature "rests on an inherently parochial foundation".
:::

---

## (ii) Dramatizing the poor

. . .

- Ethnography and intensive interviews: vivid, often shocking accounts of the daily lives of poor individuals (*Evicted*, *$2.00 a Day*, *On the Run*)

. . .

- The theory of change: humanising the poor evokes compassion, and compassion shifts the policy agenda

. . .

- Brady's critique: it overrepresents stereotypical groups, studies symptoms (eviction) rather than causes, and downplays effective policy

---

## Who is actually poor?

![Share of the U.S. population in poverty (2016–2020) that belongs to stereotypical versus typical groups. Brady (2023), Fig. 7.](figures/fig7.jpeg){.card fig-align="center" height="490"}

::: {.notes}
- Second approach: ethnography and intensive interviews that humanise the poor through vivid, often shocking narratives. Evicted, $2.00 a Day, On the Run, Gang Leader for a Day.
- Brady grants it is more construct valid than lab games, and it reveals the near-impossible choices people face.
- But three problems. (1) It overrepresents unrepresentative, "exotic" groups. Fig. 7: among people in poverty, 29.4% live in coupled working-aged households versus 18.5% in single-mother households, 57.2% in employed versus 19% in jobless households, 80.3% have zero or one risk. Black and Latino adolescents in inner cities are 1.4% and 2.3% of people in poverty. About 4% are homeless.
- The composite "typical" poor person: a white woman aged 35 to 45, high school education, coupled and employed household, no children, metropolitan area in the South.
- (2) It focuses on symptoms. Eviction: 64 times fewer people than in poverty, and "far more a symptom than a cause".
- (3) It downplays effective policy, the "fallacy of intractability". $2.00 a Day omits SNAP, which substantially reduces extreme poverty. Most people in extreme poverty are childless adults, and the biggest group of extremely poor children is in immigrant households.
- Misrepresenting the poor can backfire politically by feeding stereotypes.
:::

---

## (iii) Cultural explanations: the claim

. . .

1. People in poverty share a distinct culture: values and norms in the old version, "frames, scripts and repertoires" in the new one

. . .

2. That culture produces behaviour that keeps them poor: not finishing school, not marrying, not working

. . .

3. Poverty then reinforces the culture, and passes it on to the next generation

::: {.notes}
- A behavioural explanation with culture as the upstream cause: culture causes behaviour, behaviour causes poverty, poverty feeds back into culture.
- Old version: the "culture of poverty" of the 1960s, discredited after flawed generalisations about poor people, ethno-racial minorities and developing countries. Brady insists it fell because of logical and evidentiary problems, not only because of the Moynihan Report controversy.
- New version: in 2010 the New York Times reported "'Culture of Poverty' Makes a Comeback". Small, Harding and Lamont's Annals issue "Reconsidering culture and poverty" is among the most cited poverty research of recent decades. New vocabulary, culture described as heterogeneous and adaptive, probabilistic rather than deterministic.
- Brady's point: the argument is the same. "Rather than causing behavior, frames make it possible or likely" (Small et al.). Brady: there is no real difference between "cause" and "make possible or likely".
- Example: Harding's Living the Drama. 60 Black and Latino adolescent boys in three poor Boston neighbourhoods. "Ghetto-specific cultural models" and "negative role models" are said to lead boys not to use condoms, to engage in violence, and to "produce ignorance about how to successfully navigate educational institutions".
:::

---

## (iii) Cultural explanations: why Brady rejects them

. . .

- **Circular.** If culture causes poverty and poverty causes culture, what made poverty high in the first place?

. . .

- **No comparison.** Studies of poor people in poor neighbourhoods, with no non-poor group and no test against rival explanations

. . .

- **Wrong answer.** The evidence points to employer discrimination and segregated, lower-quality schools, not to the values of the poor

::: {.notes}
- Endogeneity: the feedback loop cannot explain the starting conditions. Cultural explanations "never really even attempted to explain systemically high poverty" and habitually omit the historical and institutional context.
- Selection: concentrating on a selectively chosen poor group without comparison groups. Harding compares disadvantaged boys and neighbourhoods against unobserved non-disadvantaged ones. Stereotypes often based on "the subjective biases of elite white male academics".
- Rival explanations: ample evidence that the poor do not hold anti-marriage or anti-school values. Rather than adolescent Black males lacking soft skills, extensive racial discrimination by employers. Rather than ignorance about college pathways, segregated and lower-quality schools and toxic environments. "It is possible that culture does not matter net of such factors."
- The new culturalists sidestep the old critiques rather than answer them, and barely mention racism: Small et al. has one mention, Harding one index entry.
- Combines the weaknesses of both other approaches: like fixing the poor, it cannot explain the high poverty that sets the stage; like dramatizing, it fixates on symptoms and overrepresents stereotypical groups.
:::

# 3. Political explanations

## {.big-center}

::: {.statement}
Poverty is a problem of **distribution**, not scarcity.
:::

. . .

::: {.statement}
Power and institutions make policy. Policy makes poverty.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Rich democracies have abundant resources. Poverty exists because they are not well distributed, and distributions are shaped by politics.
- Rank's musical chairs: too few chairs (good jobs), not the players' quickness, explains who is left standing. Brady's version: not too few chairs, one person is lying across three, several are piled broken in a corner, and someone is told there is no seat because of a "scarcity".
- Distinction from "structural" explanations (deindustrialisation, labour markets): "structuralists view poverty as the unfortunate byproduct of contextual factors ... political accounts view poverty as the willfully chosen outcome of state (in)action when something could be done."
- Rather than risks causing poverty, policy and institutions moderate the link between risks and poverty.
- Rise of this literature after about 2000, enabled by LIS data. "Poverty scholars who only know one country, know no country."
:::

---

## Social policy generosity

![Predicted poverty rates from a two-way fixed-effects model of social welfare spending (% of GDP) in 20 rich democracies, 1980–2019, with 95% CIs, overlaid with the actual U.S. minimum (1980), median (2006) and maximum (1984) poverty rates. Brady (2023), Fig. 8.](figures/fig8.jpeg){.card fig-align="center" width="85%"}

::: {.notes}
- "There has never been a country in the modern history of capitalist democracies that accomplished sustainably low poverty without a large welfare state."
- Fig. 8: two-way fixed-effects model (country, year), 20 rich democracies, 1980 to 2019, poverty on social welfare spending as a percent of GDP and its square.
- The actual US minimum (1980), median (2006) and maximum (1984) poverty rates fall almost exactly on the predicted line. The US is always in the upper left: high poverty, low spending.
- Holds whether generosity is measured as legislated social rights, transfers received, or total spending. Monetising Medicaid shows the ACA expansion reduced poverty.
- COVID: extended unemployment insurance, expanded Child Tax Credit and relief payments made poverty considerably lower.
- Implementation matters too: administrative burden, racial disparities in access.
:::

---

## Three more political themes

. . .

**Penalties are political choices.** Countries decide which risks to protect.

. . .

**Power resources.** Unions, Left parties, women in parliament push for generous policy.

. . .

**Institutions.** Slavery, segregation, federalism, criminal justice, citizenship law.

::: {.notes}
- Penalties: more than three times as much cross-national variation in single-motherhood penalties as in prevalences. The US does not have a high prevalence of single motherhood, it has the highest penalty. Not acting is a choice just like acting.
- Power resources: the default distribution of power in a capitalist democracy favours elites and business, so the less advantaged need to organise. Poverty is lower where Left parties govern, unionisation is higher, and women are a larger share of parliaments. VanHeuvelen and Brady (PSID 1976 to 2015): household union membership and state unionisation both reduce poverty and reinforce each other, spilling over to non-union households. Brady conjectures low unionisation is a more salient cause of poverty than eviction.
- Also: skepticism about the political theory behind dramatizing. No evidence that Americans are less compassionate, strong evidence they are uniquely individualistic, and no proof that poverty scholarship influences policy-makers.
- Institutions: path dependency, "residue of the power of collective actors in the past". Labour market institutions, minimum wages, citizenship rules. Immigrant-led households 22.1% poverty, noncitizen immigrant households 28.4% (Fig. 9 in backup). Baker and colleagues: nativity and citizenship explain the largest share of Latino-white and Asian-white poverty gaps.
- Racism: state-supported segregation (Massey and Denton). Baker's historical racial regimes in the South: Black poverty and the Black-white gap rise with a state's HRR score, white poverty does not. Political explanations put racism at the centre, the three prevailing approaches barely mention it (Small et al. one mention, Harding one index entry).
:::

# Conclusion

## {.big-center}

. . .

US poverty is high, stable, and everywhere

. . .

Explanations that start from the individual poor cannot account for it

. . .

Explanations that start from power, policy and institutions can

::: {.notes}
- Brady is "far from the first to criticize the individualistic problem of persons". What he documents is the empirical ascendance of political explanations, mostly since 2000 and mostly through cross-national data.
- The claim at the end: political explanations are more likely to lead to effective policy.
:::

# 4. Perspectives for psychology

## {.big-center}

::: {.statement}
Can psychology, a discipline whose unit is **the individual**, help study poverty rather than the poor?
:::

::: {.notes}
- Transition. Brady's reference list has 164 entries and almost no psychology. The implicit answer is that psychologists "pack up their things and yield the floor", as Sheehy-Skeffington and colleagues put it.
- One recent attempt at an answer: Sheehy-Skeffington, Buzan, Cano, tho Pesch and Rea (2026), Social Issues and Policy Review. Written explicitly in response to Brady.
:::

---

## A psychological reply to Brady [@sheehy-skeffingtonBringingWiderSocioecological2026]

. . .

Concedes the diagnosis: psychology has studied the behaviour of people in poverty, not poverty

. . .

Keeps the discipline: from the "i-frame" to the "s-frame"

. . .

Reverses the direction: "outside-in" rather than "inside-out"

::: {.notes}
- Their own words: "psychological research has largely fixated on what explains the behaviors of people living in poverty, rather than on what explains poverty itself (see Brady 2023)."
- Context: 15 years of growth in the psychology of poverty since Mullainathan and Shafir, with policy uptake (Behavioural Insights Team, World Bank). The authors include their own earlier work in the critique.
- i-frame and s-frame are Chater and Loewenstein's terms: explaining and intervening at the level of the individual versus the system.
- Inside-out: start from the individual in poverty, then ask what can be done around them. Outside-in: start from institutions and ideology, narrow down to the proximal experience.
- Framework: Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems (micro, meso, exo, macro), plus socioecological psychology (Oishi) and behavioural ecology, plus comparative political economy.
:::

---

## Outside-in: three layers

. . .

**Macro and exo.** Welfare regimes as "moral environments": liberal, corporatist, social-democratic, Mediterranean

. . .

**Meso.** Policy design: universal or targeted, conditional or unconditional, predistribution

. . .

**Micro.** The proximal conditions of poverty: harshness and unpredictability

::: {.notes}
- Welfare regimes (Esping-Andersen): not just resource allocation but "what it means to be a member of society". Each regime activates different schemas of dependency, autonomy, obligation.
- Liberal (US, UK): conditional "contractual citizenship", support must be earned, drug testing for TANF applicants, UK benefit sanctions linked to worse mental health. The "perversity thesis" (welfare creates poverty) works as a system-justifying ideology.
- Corporatist (Germany): deservingness organised around having "paid in". Social-democratic (Nordics): universalism, state support as solidarity, less stigma, but welfare chauvinism towards migrants. Mediterranean: families as the buffer, deservingness by traditional categories.
- Liberalisation: all regimes drifting towards the liberal model, accelerated after 2008.
- Policy design works through three psychological processes: demarcation (eligible versus not, which itself triggers stereotypes), default enrolment (administrative burden, "hurry up and wait"), dignity (having to perform worthiness as "structural violence"). Universal and unconditional provision comes out better on all three.
- Predistribution: precarious work and collective bargaining. The paper notes psychology's "lack of scholarly attention and even antagonism" towards unions, which echoes Brady's point that poverty research neglects them.
- Micro: harshness (deprivation and threat) and unpredictability (daily chaos, precarious schedules, relocation).
:::

---

## Rereading the scarcity literature

. . .

Future discounting, risk aversion, "bandwidth": **adaptive shifts** to harsh, unpredictable environments, not deficits

. . .

The flagship lab result does not survive reanalysis: "overborrowing" under scarcity reflects the task, not tunnelling

::: {.notes}
- This is the paper's answer to Brady's attack on Shah, Mullainathan and Shafir. Rather than deny the findings, reinterpret them through behavioural ecology (Frankenhuis, Nettle): when the future is uncertain and control is low, preferring sooner rewards is rational. Kidd et al.: children become more impulsive in the marshmallow test after unreliable adults.
- Poverty is then a double disadvantage: the direct harm of conditions, plus strategies that help short-term and hurt long-term.
- But the authors also warn against over-reading: structural constraints on a decision must not be mistaken for psychological shifts. A reanalysis by tho Pesch and colleagues (in press) of the Shah et al. data finds that participants in the "rich" condition rarely needed to borrow at all, so the borrowing difference reflects task design.
- They also note that some scarcity findings failed to replicate (O'Donnell et al. 2021).
- Policy conclusion from this section: "the critical point of intervention should be the environment itself."
:::

---

## Helping the poor or fighting poverty?

. . .

Interventions that help individuals move up do not lower the poverty rate

. . .

Behavioural framings may **crowd out** support for structural policy

. . .

A research agenda: deservingness and system justification, unions, universalist voting, the psychology of policymakers

::: {.notes}
- Section title is theirs. Mobility and meritocracy are valuable goals but "should not be conflated with the goal of reducing poverty at the population level". That is Brady's musical chairs restated.
- The "psychological poverty trap" assumption is called "empirically unsubstantiated" at the population level, with Brady's cross-national evidence as the reason.
- Crowding out: Hagmann et al. 2019, making people aware of a green-energy nudge reduced support for a carbon tax. The paper extends the worry to poverty, with Chater and Loewenstein. Both papers compare poverty to climate change as a structural problem.
- Luck egalitarianism: the option-luck versus brute-luck distinction collapses once choices are constrained by the socioecology, so "voluntary" choices of the poor carry the responsibilities of others.
- Where psychology could enter Brady's framework: the public psychology that sustains penalties (deservingness, perversity thesis), participation in unions and collective movements, voting for egalitarian platforms, and why policymakers fail to implement what they advocate.
- Closing line of the paper: psychology as part "not only of making poverty tolerable or escapable, but of ending it altogether."
:::

# 5. Discussion

## Discussion points

::: {.incremental}
- Is "outside-in" a new question or the old question with more context variables? Where does the individual remain the unit of analysis in Sheehy-Skeffington et al.?

- Deficit versus adaptation: does reinterpreting scarcity effects as adaptive move the lever to the environment, or just make the behavioural story more sympathetic?

- Shah et al. 2012 is hit twice, conceptually by Brady and empirically by the reanalysis. What survives of the scarcity-mindset programme?

- Both papers claim narratives have political effects (dramatizing backfires, nudges crowd out structural support). Neither tests it for poverty. Could we?

- Climate is the analogy both papers reach for. Is the individual-behaviour framing of climate action the trap Brady describes, and are we in it?
:::

::: {.notes}
- Point 1: a third of the new paper is still the microsystem and "psychological shifts". Brady would call that studying the poor.
- Point 2: the authors' own caution applies: structural constraints on a decision are not psychological shifts.
- Point 3: Brady's objection is construct validity (video games as scarcity) and that feedback loops cannot explain why the US has high poverty in the first place. The reanalysis adds that the task itself produced the effect.
- Point 4: Brady says it "has never really been proven" that poverty scholarship moves policy-makers or public opinion. Hagmann et al. is the climate template. A poverty version is a feasible survey experiment.
- Point 5: link to the megastudy. Interventions that move an attitude without moving downstream outcomes, and the question of which goal an individual-level intervention serves.
:::

## Child poverty over time

![Child poverty rates for Black (solid), Latino (dashed) and white (dotted) children in the United States, 1970–2019, with 95% CIs. Brady (2023), Fig. 4.](figures/fig4.jpeg){.card fig-align="center" width="85%"}

::: {.notes}
- Black child poverty near 50% and Latino child poverty above 45% in the mid-1980s, an increase from the 1970s. Only recently down to near 30%.
- "Most Black and Latino adults today grew up experiencing truly extraordinarily high poverty during childhood compared to any rich democracy in over four decades of the LIS."
:::

---

## Immigrant and citizenship status

![Poverty rates by immigrant and citizenship status of the household, United States (2016–2020) versus the cross-national median of 24 rich democracies. Dotted line: CN median for the overall population. Brady (2023), Fig. 9.](figures/fig9.jpeg){.card fig-align="center" height="490"}

::: {.notes}
- Immigrant-led households in the US: 22.1%. Citizen immigrant households similar to the overall population. Noncitizen immigrant households: 28.4%.
- Citizenship laws and their enforcement block access to social policy, constrain employment rights, and limit residential choices. Immigrants may be "the most understudied population in poverty in the United States".
:::
